agree.reason: The calm tone and the 74-household figure work against the idea that this is a few loud people, but the letter offers nothing in return (no weekday-evening meetings, no list of residents who need help on the stairs) and leaves out the missed dialysis appointments, so a manager who thinks the company has done well has little reason to move.

honest.reason: Every number matches the brief and "about two-thirds" is accurate (74/112), though the letter never says the association can't speak for all 112 households.

works_the_facts.reason: The only derived figure is two-thirds; the letter never turns 41 days into a share of the year, never notes that June plus 6–8 weeks has already passed several times over, and never says what continued outages would mean.

right_comparison.reason: It contrasts the part promised in June with the same promise now and explains why a safety certificate is not proof of reliability, but it never sets out what the next months look like if nothing changes.

qualification.reason: Deadlines are left as "[date]", and nothing says what the association will do if the part doesn't arrive or management doesn't answer, so the reader has no checkable condition or consequence.

objections.reason: It answers the inspection-certificate defence well and handles the $400,000 claim fairly by asking for the assessment, but it misses the user's real requests (stair-climbing chair, rent credit) and doesn't address the "loud few" view beyond the petition count.

fit.reason: At about 400 words it is the right length and form for an open letter, but names, address, date and contact are placeholders the user could have supplied, so it isn't ready to post or send to the station.
